title: InfinityStar: Uniﬁed Spacetime AutoRegressive Modeling for Visual Generatio

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states that 'clips are generated sequentially conditioned on prior clip predictions and the text input in an autoregressive manner,' implying the joint distribution should condition on tokens from all previous clips (r^{<c}). However, Eq. (2) is written as ∏_{c=1}^{N} ∏_{k=1}^{K} p(r_k^c | r_1^c,...,r_{k-1}^c, ψ(t)), which only conditions on tokens within the same clip c and the text embedding, omitting any dependence on tokens from previous clips (c'<c). As written, this factorization describes clips as conditionally independent given the text, contradicting the paper's central claim of inter-clip autoregression and the ability to 'generate infinitely long videos theoretically' by conditioning on prior clips.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract / Introduction vs. Section 4.5 and Table 6
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract claims InfinityStar 'generates a 5s, 720p video approximately 10× faster than leading diffusion-based methods,' and the Introduction repeats 'InfinityStar achieves a 10× reduction in inference latency relative to leading diffusion models' using 'tokenizers of the same compression rate.' However, Section 4.5 and Table 6 report that InfinityStar achieves a 32× speedup over Wan-2.1 under the same 5s/720p/81-frame setting ('Even without employing stronger compression, InfinityStar achieves a 32× speedup over Wan-2.1'). The 10× figure directly contradicts the 32× figure measured under ostensibly the same conditions.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 1, citation [38] referring to 'the VBench benchmark [38]'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text repeatedly cites VBench as reference [38] ('On the VBench benchmark [38], InfinityStar establishes...'), but the corresponding reference list entry [38] is 'F. Zhang, S. Tian, Z. Huang, Y. Qiao, and Z. Liu. Evaluation Agent: Efficient and Promptable Evaluation Framework for Visual Generative Models. arXiv:2412.09645, 2024.' This is a different paper (Evaluation Agent) from the actual VBench benchmark paper (Huang et al., 'VBench: Comprehensive Benchmark Suite for Video Generative Models'), constituting a misattributed/incorrect citation for a benchmark central to the paper's main results.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 6, footnote 'Note: Baselines evaluated at different resolutions and model sizes'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The note claims baselines were evaluated at 'different resolutions,' but the table itself lists identical resolution (720p), identical duration (5s), and identical frame count (81 frames) for all three methods (Wan 2.1, Nova, InfinityStar). Only model size actually differs across rows, so the caveat about 'different resolutions' is not supported by (and contradicts) the table's own data.

The abstract states InfinityStar achieves 83.74 on VBench, 'marginally outperforming selected autoregressive models, and comparable to leading diffusion competitors such as HunyuanVideo.' Per Table 2, the gap over autoregressive baselines (Emu3 80.96, Nova 80.12) is 2.8–3.6 points, which is substantial in VBench terms, while the gap over HunyuanVideo (83.24) is only 0.5 points, i.e., genuinely marginal. The abstract's characterization inverts the actual magnitude of these differences, describing the larger AR improvement as 'marginal' and the marginal diffusion improvement as merely 'comparable.'

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 2, Appearance Style column for Emu3 and Nova
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Emu3 and Nova, two different autoregressive models with very different Human Action, Scene, Multiple Objects, Quality, and Semantic scores, report an identical Appearance Style score of 20.92, which is suspicious given no other model pair in the table shares an identical value for any metric, suggesting a possible copy-paste/data-entry error rather than a genuine coincidence.
